one_liner: Vector-backed hash map beating std::unordered_map on build, iteration, and string-key workloads, with weaker reference stability.
what_it_does: An (almost) drop-in replacement for std::unordered_map and std::unordered_set: same STL container API, but elements are stored contiguously in a std::vector instead of per-node allocations, with a separate index pointing into it. Also ships segmented_map/segmented_set (fixed-size segments, values never reallocate) and huge_page:: variants that MADV_HUGEPAGE large blocks. Solves the same associative-lookup problem as std::unordered_map, traded for cache-friendly storage and near-free full-table iteration.
how_it_is_fast: Values live in a std::vector, so iteration is a linear scan with no pointer chasing. Lookups use a separate flat array of 88-byte 'group' blocks (16 slots each: 16 one-byte fingerprints, 8 overflow counters, 16 value indices); a probe loads all 16 fingerprints and compares them in one SSE2 (x86-64) or NEON (AArch64) instruction. Overflow counters replace tombstones, so erase never forces a rehash. Inserts emplace_back onto the vector and record the slot in the index, keeping iteration order equal to insertion order until an erase reorders it.
when_to_use: Workloads that iterate the whole table often (snapshotting, serialization, aggregation) — 0.19 ns/element vs 21.29 for std::unordered_map (~110x) and 5.5-13x faster than flat hash maps like abseil/boost
std::string-keyed maps that are built and torn down repeatedly — 2.1-2.6x faster build+destroy than any flat map measured (93 ns/entry vs 192-237 ns)
Need to debug/inspect the table's contents easily — data is a plain std::vector, visible in any debugger, plus a bundled LLDB formatter script

Want a std::unordered_map-shaped container with pluggable storage: std::allocator, polymorphic allocators, a custom random-access container (e.g. boost::interprocess::vector), or a huge-page allocator
Batch key lookups against a large or partially-missing key set — visit() gives 1.15-1.5x over one-at-a-time find() by overlapping independent memory accesses
when_not_to_use: Code that depends on iterator or reference stability across insert/erase — elements live in a std::vector, so growth reallocates and erase moves the last element into the freed slot
Integer-keyed, find- or churn-dominated workloads where every ns counts — loses to boost::unordered_flat_map on u64 find (0.73x) and churn (0.61x), and to abseil's flat_hash_map similarly
Erase-heavy workloads specifically — erase needs two lookups (the target slot and the slot of the element swapped into it), called out in the README as "relatively slow"

Any code path where a value's destructor (or other callback) re-enters erase() on the same map while an erase is already in progress — this infinite-loops; the maintainer says it is unsupported and won't be fixed (GitHub issue #126)
Need const Key in the stored pair (std::pair<const Key, Value>) — this map's pair has a non-const key, unlike std::unordered_map

integration.dependencies: none (include/ankerl/unordered_dense.h + include/ankerl/stl.h; huge_page_allocator.h is a separate optional header needing <sys/mman.h>)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 for map/set; C++20 required only for the optional module build (import ankerl.unordered_dense)
integration.platforms: x86-64 (SSE2 probe, part of the baseline, no flag needed), AArch64 (NEON probe, likewise automatic); any other architecture falls back to a portable word-at-a-time probe via ANKERL_UNORDERED_DENSE_HAS_SSE2/NEON=0. huge_page_allocator degrades to std::allocator on Windows/macOS.
integration.thread_safety: not documented — no built-in synchronization; standard container assumptions apply (concurrent reads are fine, no writer may run concurrently with any other access)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: same STL-style API as std::unordered_map/set for nearly everything, but no const Key in the pair, weaker iterator/reference stability on insert/erase, and erase() is not reentrant

gotchas: No iterator or reference stability on insert or erase — elements live in a std::vector, so any growth or erase can relocate other elements
Reentrant erase() (e.g. a destructor triggered by that very erase calling erase() again on the same map) infinite-loops; maintainer confirmed this is unsupported and won't be fixed (issue #126)

A custom hash functor without `using is_avalanching = void;` is silently treated as low-quality and gets an extra mixing step; forgetting the marker on a genuinely good hash costs speed with no warning (require_avalanching<Hash> exists to make this a compile error instead)

Post-5.0 the index is one 88-byte block per 16 slots (5.5-9.5 bytes/slot depending on bucket_type), not one bucket per slot as in 4.x — code carried over from 4.x that computes memory as bucket_count() * sizeof(bucket_type) still compiles but silently gives the wrong number; use index_bytes() instead
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick unordered_dense over abseil::flat_hash_map or boost::unordered_flat_map when iteration speed or std::string-keyed build/destroy dominate (its 0.19 ns/element iterate and ~93 ns/entry string build+destroy beat both); pick abseil or boost instead when integer-keyed find/churn throughput is what matters, since unordered_dense loses to boost there (0.73x find, 0.61x churn) and to abseil similarly. Against folly's F14ValueMap, unordered_dense wins on both build+destroy (4.84x vs 3.97x) and find (1.98x vs 1.72x) per this catalog's numbers. robin_hood::unordered_map is an earlier project by the same author with a different (robin-hood) index; unordered_dense's 5.0 index replaced that design and is reported 1.6x faster build+destroy than it on u64 keys, per doc/benchmarks.md.
verified_claims_summary: On the library's own scripts/ab/bench_readme.sh harness (clang 22.1.8, -O3, transparent huge pages via madvise, pinned to one core, Fedora 44, AMD Ryzen 9 7950X; std::unordered_map presumed on libstdc++) with 1-2 million u64 or std::string keys, ankerl::unordered_dense::map beat std::unordered_map by 4.84x on build+destroy, 1.98x on find, 2.84x on churn, and roughly 110x on full-table iteration (0.19 vs 21.29 ns/element); with std::string keys build+destroy was 3.64x faster. This is a first-party benchmark — the author wrote both the map and the harness, which he states on the page — but the harness, raw CSV, and SVGs are public in the repo.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-23, 1,482 stars, CMakeLists shows current release 5.0.1); MIT-licensed, header-only, and used in production projects including MySQL and PrusaSlicer per doc/users.md.
